_comment: Production series, film 1. Slides only (no recording).

description.en: How FundsXML runs in production: who sends what to whom, the whole delivery chain on one page (sources, central database, generator, validation, SFTP, API and portals), the chains of sender and receiver, security, rhythms and schema versions, the five building blocks of a production setup, roles, build or buy, two environments, document IDs, and the complete example used in this series, which can be downloaded.

say.en: FundsXML in production: how do the files get from one system into another, every day, reliably? In this film you see who sends what to whom, the delivery chain on both sides, how files travel, and the building blocks every production setup needs.

Start with the parties. The asset manager and the fund administrator produce most of the data: master data, prices, portfolios and regulatory templates. The custodian adds holdings and transactions. Platforms and distributors, insurers and data vendors receive. Many companies are on both sides: an insurer receives portfolios, and sends its own reports on.

en.title: Each receiver needs a different part

items.head: Platforms and data vendors
items.text: Prices, net asset values, master data.

items.head: Insurers
items.text: The full portfolio and the TPT for Solvency II.

items.head: One sender
items.text: Several kinds of deliveries from the same data.

say.en: Each receiver needs a different part. Platforms and data vendors need prices and master data. Insurers need the full portfolio and the Tripartite Template for Solvency two. Distributors need the European MiFID and E S G templates, and documents. One sender therefore produces several kinds of deliveries from the same data.

On the sender's side, the chain has five steps. Extract the data from the source systems: fund accounting, portfolio management, master data. Map it to the FundsXML structure. Generate the file. Validate it, against the schema and against business rules. And deliver it to the receivers.

en.title: A delivery chain on one page

say.en: Here is the whole chain on one page. The data rarely comes from one system. Net asset values come from fund accounting, positions from the portfolio system, identifiers and names from master data. A good setup collects them in one place first, often a database, where the data is checked once. From there, a generator writes the file each partner needs, it is validated, and it travels by S F T P, through an A P I or to a portal.

items.head: Corrections in one place
items.text: The history shows what was sent when.

items.head: The same numbers for every partner
items.text: No two different NAVs for the same day.

say.en: Why one central place? Because the data is checked once and then used for every partner. Corrections are made in one place, and the history shows what was sent when. And every partner gets the same numbers, which avoids the classic problem of two receivers with two different net asset values for the same day.

Follow one net asset value through the chain. At six in the evening, fund accounting calculates it. At eight, it is approved. At ten, the file is generated and validated, and a quarter of an hour later it is on its way. At seven the next morning, the platform has loaded it, and by nine, investors see the new price. Every step has a time, and every step can be late.

On the receiver's side, the chain mirrors the sender's. Receive the file. Validate it, before anything else. Load it into the own systems. Reconcile it: do the numbers fit together and with what you already know? And send feedback to the sender, especially when something is wrong.

items.head: SFTP
items.text: Most common, on a fixed schedule.

items.head: Portals
items.text: Run by platforms and data vendors.

items.head: E-mail
items.text: Hard to automate and monitor: the exception.

say.en: How does the file travel? Most often by S F T P, on a fixed schedule. More and more partners offer an A P I. Fund platforms and data vendors often run their own portals. E-mail is still common, but it is hard to automate and to monitor, so it should be the exception.

items.head: Upload, then rename
items.text: The receiver never picks up half a file.

say.en: With S F T P, a few rules prevent most problems. Agree on file names that contain the sender, the kind of data and the date. Upload under a temporary name and rename the file when it is complete, so that the receiver never picks up half a file. Compress large files. And use keys per partner, never shared passwords.

Fund data is often confidential, portfolios in particular. Transport is always encrypted. Where proof of origin matters, a FundsXML file can carry an XML signature; the schema supports it. Every file sent and received goes into an archive. And access to the data is limited to the people and systems that need it.

Different data has a different rhythm. Prices and net asset values go out daily, often with an agreed cut-off time, for example by ten in the morning. Portfolios are often monthly. Master data, documents and regulatory templates go out when they change. And corrections go out whenever they are needed. Each delivery is its own file, with its own document ID.

items.head: Two or three versions at a time
items.text: One for each group of receivers.

say.en: Not every partner uses the same schema version. A sender often writes two or three versions at the same time, one for each group of receivers. That needs a clear list of which partner gets which version and which templates, tests for every version, and a plan for moving partners to a new version together.

Whatever the tools, every production setup needs five building blocks. A scheduler that starts the deliveries on time. Validation on both sides. An archive of every file sent and received. Monitoring that notices when a file is late or wrong. And a partner register that knows who gets what.

Technology is only half of it. Someone must own the chain. The data owners answer for the content: whether a price is right, and who corrects it. Operations runs the daily deliveries and talks to the partners. And I T looks after the systems, the transfers and security. When these roles are clear, problems are solved in minutes instead of days.

Some architectures cause trouble sooner or later. A separate script for every partner, each one a little different. Manual steps in the middle of the night. No archive, so nobody can say what was sent. Checks only at the receiver, so errors travel first. And no monitoring, so a missing file is noticed by the partner, not by you.

items.head: Buy
items.text: Data management and distribution platforms, many speak FundsXML.

items.head: Mixed
items.text: A vendor for distribution, own checks on top.

say.en: Build or buy? Some companies build the chain themselves, with a database and scheduled jobs. Others use the data management or distribution platforms of specialised vendors, many of which speak FundsXML. A common middle way: a vendor for distribution, and the own checks on top. Either way, the building blocks stay the same.

items.head: Test
items.text: New partners, versions and changes, with example data and test partners.

items.head: Kept apart
items.text: Same code; separate data, keys and addresses.

say.en: Every chain needs at least two environments. A test environment, where new partners, new versions and changes are tried with example data and test partners. And production, with the real partners. Both run the same code, but with separate data, separate keys and separate addresses, so that a test file can never reach a real partner.

items.head: A simple pattern
items.text: Supplier – kind of delivery – date – sequence.

items.head: A resend keeps its ID
items.text: A corrected file gets a new one.

say.en: Plan the document IDs carefully, because everything downstream relies on them. An ID must be unique forever. A simple pattern works well: the supplier, the kind of delivery, the date and a sequence number. A resend of the same file keeps its ID; a corrected file gets a new one. Never reuse an ID, not even after years.

items.head: Generator
items.text: One file per partner, in schema order.

items.head: Validate
items.text: XSD 1.1, in CI on every change.

say.en: For the next films we use a complete example, published in the FundsXML examples repository on GitHub: a PostgreSQL database, a loader for FundsXML files and a generator back to FundsXML, with six sample deliveries and the files it writes for three partners. It is an example, not a product, but it shows the essential steps, and you can download it and run it yourself.
That was the delivery chain on both sides. In the next film, you see how FundsXML data is stored in a database. Thanks for watching.
